title: A first variational classifier
source: Lecture 10 Building a Quantum Classifier 1.pdf, PDF pages 17–22, 31 and 33–42. Supplemental one-qubit example.
objectives: Separate data encoding from trainable parameters.
Read a probability as a model prediction.
Compute an expectation gradient by parameter shift.
body:
A quantum model inside a classical loop

Encode a scalar feature x with Rᵧ(x), apply a trainable Rᵧ(w), then measure. Starting from |0⟩, the probability of label 1 is p(1|x,w) = sin²((x+w)/2). A classical optimizer updates w to reduce a loss over training examples.

This tiny model combines the two rotations into one. It is an intentionally limited teaching model that a classical computer simulates easily. It demonstrates the training loop and makes no claim of quantum advantage.

From probability to expectation

The Z expectation is f(x,w)=1−2p(1|x,w)=cos(x+w). For this rotation, ∂f/∂w = [f(x,w+π/2)−f(x,w−π/2)]/2. A loss gradient still needs the chain rule; shifting the whole loss is not generally the same calculation.

Evaluate the complete experiment

Fit preprocessing on training data only. Keep a test set for final evaluation. Compare classical baselines and report circuit depth, sampling cost, seeds, and uncertainty.

Explore before training

Move x and w to predict the circuit output. The notebook implements Qiskit statevector predictions, parameter-shift gradients, a small training loop, and a held-out comparison.

quiz.question: For x=0 and w=π, what is p(1)?

exercise: Derive ∂p(1|x,w)/∂w. Explain why changing the number of shots changes uncertainty but not the ideal probability.
solution: ∂p/∂w = sin(x+w)/2. For N independent shots the estimated probability has variance p(1−p)/N.
